specPoints.text: understand that a disproportionation reaction involves an element in a single species being simultaneously oxidised and reduced

primer.text: Some reactions split one species against itself: a single element is pushed up and down the oxidation ladder at the same time. That double life is disproportionation. This note defines it, walks the chlorine-in-alkali case ion by ion, and shows the five-step balancing routine that turns observation into a tidy equation.

lessons.title: One element, two directions
lessons.opening: Disproportionation is a split personality reaction: a single element inside one species simultaneously climbs and falls on the oxidation ladder. This lesson defines the phenomenon and shows the chlorine-in-water case where one chlorine atom oxidises another from the same starting molecule.
keyPoints: A disproportionation reaction involves one species being simultaneously oxidised and reduced.
The same element divides into two products at different oxidation numbers.
In chlorine water, Cl2 splits into chloride at -1 and chlorate(I) at +1.
The starting element sits at 0, exactly between the two destinations.
Both a reduction leg and an oxidation leg run inside one reaction.

low.restatement: One species starts at one oxidation number and ends split across two - one leg up, one leg down - which is why the reaction is named dis-proportion-ation: the proportions divide.
low.analogy: One ladder, two climbers: the same person's identical twins start on the same rung, and one steps up while the other steps down at the same instant.
low.examPointer: Quote both destination states with signs when identifying disproportionation - one up and one down from the same start is the whole signature.

medium.restatement: The element's initial state must sit between its two product states; the electron ledger closes internally because the electrons lost on the oxidation leg are exactly those gained on the reduction leg, with no outside partner needed.
medium.analogy: A self-contained transaction: the same account splits its balance, transferring internally so the books balance without any external counterparty.
medium.examPointer: If asked why a species cannot disproportionate, show it lacks an accessible state on both sides of its current one.

options.text: One species is simultaneously oxidised and reduced
options.explanation: The split into two directions is the defining signature.
That is ordinary redox between partners.

options.text: A species neither gains nor loses electrons
options.explanation: No transfer means no redox at all.
Displacement is a different reaction family.

check.stem: In chlorine water, which products does chlorine divide into?

options.explanation: One leg down, one leg up from 0.
The second product must carry a different state.
That belongs to the hot-alkali case, not chlorine water.
Oxygen is not the split partner here.

check.stem: Why must the starting oxidation state sit between the two product states?

options.text: One leg must go up and one leg down for simultaneous oxidation and reduction
options.explanation: The split requires an accessible state on both sides.
No such prohibition exists.
Physical state is irrelevant.

options.text: So the equation balances by mass
options.explanation: Mass balance is automatic; the state geometry is the point.

check.stem: Which statement about the electron ledger in disproportionation is correct?

options.text: Electrons lost on the oxidation leg exactly equal those gained on the reduction leg
options.explanation: The ledger closes inside one species.

options.text: External ions supply the missing electrons
options.explanation: No external partner exists.

options.text: Electrons appear as free particles in the products
options.explanation: Electrons never appear in balanced equations.

options.text: The legs run in separate vessels
options.explanation: The legs run in one reaction mixture.

check.stem: Which of these is NOT required to identify a reaction as disproportionation?

options.text: A metal catalyst speeding the reaction
options.explanation: Catalysis plays no role in the definition.

options.text: A single species containing the element
options.explanation: The reactant must hold one relevant species.

options.text: One product at a higher oxidation number
options.explanation: The upward leg is required.

options.text: One product at a lower oxidation number
options.explanation: The downward leg is required.

check.stem: State the definition of a disproportionation reaction.
check.modelAnswer: Disproportionation is the reaction type in which a single species is oxidised and reduced at the same instant, splitting one element across two products.

check.stem: Give the two oxidation numbers chlorine lands on in chlorine water.
check.modelAnswer: Chlorine lands on -1 as chloride and +1 as chlorate(I), split from its starting 0.

check.stem: Explain why disproportionation needs no external oxidising or reducing agent.
check.modelAnswer: The species supplies both roles: some of its atoms lose electrons and some gain them, so the electron ledger closes internally within one reactant.

check.stem: Chlorine water splits Cl at 0 into -1 and +1. If one chlorine atom oxidises by 1 unit, how many must reduce by 1 unit to close the ledger?
check.modelAnswer: One atom losing 1 electron feeds exactly one atom gaining 1 electron, so the split is one-to-one in that case.

lessons.title: Balancing chlorine in hot alkali, step by step
lessons.opening: The five-step routine turns observation into a balanced equation. This lesson walks chlorine through hot concentrated sodium hydroxide to chloride and chlorate(V), watching the oxidation numbers drive every coefficient.
keyPoints: Step 1 writes the unbalanced equation and flags the atoms that change oxidation number.
Step 2 deduces the changes: chlorine falls 0 to -1 and climbs 0 to +5.
Step 3 balances the ledger: one atom up 5 needs five atoms down 1.
Step 4 balances charge with hydroxide ions, and step 5 balances atoms with water.

low.restatement: Write the skeleton, read the state changes off chlorine, scale so the up-leg equals the down-leg, patch charge with hydroxide, then patch atoms with water until everything closes.
low.analogy: Repairing a see-saw: first spot which rider moved (states), then add counterweights (coefficients) until both sides level out (balance).
low.examPointer: Never skip step 2 - writing the 0 to -1 and 0 to +5 changes explicitly is where the method marks live.

medium.restatement: The 5-unit climb per chlorine to chlorate(V) demands five 1-unit falls to chloride, fixing the 5Cl- to 1ClO3- ratio; six hydroxides then deliver six negative charges matching the six product ions, and three waters absorb the leftover hydrogens and oxygens.
medium.analogy: A payroll where one manager draws a 5-unit bonus paid by five staff at 1 unit each - the coefficients are the headcount the ledger forces.
medium.examPointer: Check the final equation by atom census: 6 Cl, 6 O and 6 H appear on each side - a failed census means a wrong coefficient upstream.

check.stem: In hot concentrated NaOH, chlorine ends as which two ions?

options.explanation: Chloride and chlorate(V) are the hot-alkali destinations.
That is the cold, dilute alkali case.
No hydrogen product appears in this reaction.
Those are reactants, not products.

check.stem: Which oxidation-number changes drive the balancing?

options.text: Chlorine falls 0 to -1 and climbs 0 to +5
options.explanation: One down-leg and one up-leg define the split.
Disproportionation needs both legs.
Oxygen stays -2 throughout.
Sodium is a spectator ion here.

check.stem: Why does the 5Cl- to 1ClO3- ratio appear in the balanced equation?

options.text: One chlorine climbs 5 units, so five chlorines must each fall 1 unit to balance the ledger
options.explanation: The electron ledger fixes the headcount.
Mass plays no role in the ratio's origin.

options.text: The chlorate ion holds five oxygens
options.explanation: It holds three, and oxygens do not set the ratio.
The alkali supplies charge balance, not the chlorine headcount.

check.stem: How many hydroxide ions appear on the reactant side, and why?

options.text: Six, matching the six negative charges among the products
options.explanation: Step 4 patches charge with hydroxide.
The waters belong to step 5, not the charge patch.
The chlorides carry only part of the product charge.
The ionic form exposes the hydroxide's role.

check.stem: What final census verifies the balanced equation 3Cl2 + 6OH- -> 5Cl- + ClO3- + 3H2O?

options.text: 6 chlorine, 6 oxygen and 6 hydrogen atoms on each side
options.explanation: The full atom census closes on both sides.
Three Cl2 molecules hold six atoms.
Three waters plus one chlorate hold six.
Both atoms and charges must close.

check.stem: List the five steps for balancing a disproportionation equation.
check.modelAnswer: Write the unbalanced equation, deduce the oxidation-number changes, balance the number changes, balance the charges, then balance the atoms.

check.stem: Write the balanced equation for chlorine in hot concentrated sodium hydroxide.
check.modelAnswer: 3Cl2 + 6OH- -> 5Cl- + ClO3- + 3H2O closes the chlorine, oxygen and hydrogen censuses.

check.stem: Explain why the hot-alkali product differs from the cold-dilute product.
check.modelAnswer: Reaction conditions decide which split chlorine takes: hot concentrated alkali pushes the oxidation leg all the way to chlorate(V) at +5, while cold dilute alkali stops it at chlorate(I) at +1.

check.stem: In the balanced hot-alkali equation, how many electrons move in total per 3 chlorine molecules reacting?
check.modelAnswer: Five atoms fall 1 unit and one climbs 5, so 5 electrons shift per 6 chlorine atoms - matching a 5-unit up-leg and 5-unit down-leg total.

glossary.definition: A reaction in which one species is simultaneously oxidised and reduced, splitting one element across two product states.
The ClO3- ion, where chlorine sits at oxidation number +5 and forms in hot concentrated alkali.
The electron bookkeeping that balances every unit climbed against every unit fallen in a redox equation.

workedExample.prompt: Balance the disproportionation of chlorine in hot concentrated aqueous sodium hydroxide, where the products are Cl-, ClO3- and water.
steps: Step 1 - write the skeleton: Cl2 -> Cl- + ClO3- and flag chlorine as the changing atom.
Step 2 - deduce the changes: chlorine falls from 0 to -1 and climbs from 0 to +5.
Step 3 - balance the ledger: one atom climbing 5 units needs five atoms falling 1 unit, so 5Cl- per ClO3-.
Step 4 - balance charge: 6OH- on the left matches the 6 negative charges among 5Cl- and ClO3-.
Step 5 - balance atoms: 3H2O absorbs the 6 hydrogens and 3 extra oxygens, giving 3Cl2 + 6OH- -> 5Cl- + ClO3- + 3H2O.
workedExample.finalAnswer: 3Cl2 + 6OH- -> 5Cl- + ClO3- + 3H2O, with chlorine split 5 down to -1 and 1 up to +5.
